utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone and a thank you to both parties for attending this afternoon. This is not like a hearing in court, and standing up for the Judges coming into this sort of meeting is not necessary. The whole idea is that everyone should feel as comfortable as possible in this environment, if that means taking your jacket and your tie off, then that you should do. The first thing I think it's appropriate for us to deal with this afternoon is the identification of everyone who is in the room. The Prosecution are familiar with all the Judges of the Tribunal. Mr. Karadzic, you've encountered me, and you've encountered Judge Flugge on one occasion already. We also have with us Judge Picard today, and we also have two of the legal support team, the other two young ladies here who I work with, the Trial Chamber, Ms. Davidson on my left who is the most senior of the two, and Ms. Hinek who is behind. And they will be a regular feature of any meetings of this nature; or a Status Conference, for example, you'll have seen both of them in court at your previous appearances. Can we now hear from the Prosecution who represents them this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution to my right we have the trial attorneys Ms. Sutherland, and Mr. Nicholls. They are also new to you, and to everyone here. And to my left is the case manager, Mr. Reid, and I'm Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, you had reservations about coming to this meeting, and because of that we thought it appropriate to set out -- or at least discuss how we might proceed in future in dealing with the management of your case and the preparation of your case for trial. We had already, prior to that, decided that the three judges should attend this meeting. In future cases that will not always happen. It's not generally the case. It's normally the case that only the pre-trial judge, who in this case is myself, would attend, but this is a case with many issues involved. It's a large case. It's only right that we should set a course initially that everyone contributes to any orders about how we proceed will not be made today. They will be made in a transparent context in court. There will be a Status Conference on the 2nd of April. But this meeting gives an opportunity for everyone involved to express their views on how we might best achieve the objective of a fair and expeditious trial which is our obligation to you. The initial order of the 19th of March confirming this meeting, actually describes the purpose of a Rule 65 ter meeting in fairly clear terms. The order provides that Rule 65 ter paragraph D establishes a framework for meetings to be held regularly between the parties in order to discuss practical matters of trial preparation under the supervision of the pre-trial judge and/or the senior legal officer of the Chamber. These meetings are generally conducted in private and do not form part of the trial process, rather they are for the purpose of effective trial preparation in a context where the parties are encouraged to discuss matters freely without risk to the safety of witnesses by inadvertent reference to confidential material. A transcript will be kept and provided to you and to the Prosecution. Normally these meetings take place with counsel and not with the accused, but in this case because you represent yourself, these meetings have inevitably to involve you. Now, what I think you will find this afternoon, I hesitate to predict too much because I don't have a very clear picture of how much information will emerge; but what I think you'll find is that we will both obtain useful information for our respective purposes in making progress in this case. That you will not be obliged in any way to commit yourself to something about which you have any reservations. That will only take place in a public setting. And you will have the opportunity, yourself, to raise matters subject to our supervision with the Prosecution. They may wish to ask matters of you. I suspect on this first occasion that there's unlikely to be much raised by them of you that we would authorise or oblige you to deal with. But there will come a stage where we will, I think, expect mutual cooperation to everyone's advantage. But later that's further down the line in the course of preparations for the trial. Now, before asking the Prosecution to comment, if they wish at all, on how we should proceed in future; can I ask whether you wish to make any comments about how we ought to conduct these meetings and how they might be related to the Status Conferences which will occur from time to time in the courtroom in a formal setting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to say that I don't mind meeting with this distinguished company; but until I am declared to be an innocent and free man, any socialising outside of the public eye could only be to my prejudice, I could not benefit from it at all. I think that the public is a very important element of my Defence, and I'm convinced that I may not deviate from that. I came here not only out of good manners and the respect that I have for you. I also came here to hear what's going to be said here, but I will not present my positions, my views. I will leave that for a later date once I have studied the transcript, and I will present my views in a public hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is there anything you wish to say on the first item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I only want to mention that the Prosecution would really appreciate these kind of meetings because we can not -- we have no Defence counsel with whom we can sit together and discuss practical matters, not substantive matters but practical matters; and we hope that this forum here would be an opportunity to basically engage in these practical matters with Mr. Karadzic in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's return to that subject at the end of the meeting once you see what, if anything, can be achieved by this exercise. The second item that we identified was clarification of arrangements for the disclosure of material relating to expert witnesses. And the Prosecution have already provided a list of experts which is helpful but raises a very large number of questions in the minds of the Judges on which we would like some clarification, and I'd be surprised if it hasn't raised a lot of questions in your mind as well, on which I hope we can actually get some clarification. In three cases now, the Prosecution have filed a formal notice with a view to triggering the period of 30 days that you have in which to answer or to challenge these reports. The three are, in case you are in doubt, Christian Nielsen, Andras Riedlmayer, and Kathryn Barr; and I will deal with these three first of all. And deal with them separately. And the first of these is Christian Nielsen. Now, the Trial Chamber at the moment only has the notice along with this summary list produced by the Prosecution. Once we are clear what documents are to be relied on for the purpose of the trial, and that may change following this meeting, hopefully, the Trial Chamber would benefit from having these documents. Now, you've got obligations to the accused, but you don't have any obligations towards us at this stage in that regard, unless we make an order. We'd rather not do that, and we'd rather simply request that when a document that is going to be relied upon as evidence in the trial, and that applies to expert reports, statements, and curriculum vitae, then we would like to have a copy. Now, do you have any objections to giving us copies at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Your Honour. Actually, our plan was to as soon as we have a reaction to -- from Mr. Karadzic whether he wants to cross-examine these people, we actually had intended to then file the report with the Trial Chamber. But we can easily also always attach it already to the notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be helpful but that's because we are concerned about the final format in which you present this material. It is -- just to stray a moment more widely into the list, it's very disturbing to read about a witness in respect of whom there are 29 reports and addenda, and that awaited translations amount to 1.226 pages. That for us is horrific information, and therefore seeing that would provide some -- perhaps some reassurance when you tender the notice; but perhaps as we go through this today, these figures may change and if in fact we all agree at the end that it's best that you give us the documents once it's clear whether they are going to be challenged, then so be it. But I suspect it will probably be better to have the information earlier. In any event, if we can look at Christian Nielsen, where your summary suggested that there were three reports. You have in fact produced two, and you presumably have had everything translated now so that the part of the summary that refers to 12 pages awaiting translation is, I assume now redundant.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We still have -- no, no, that's right for Mr. Nielsen we have everything translated, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the reports and addenda now total two rather than three; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, because one of these reports that we originally had in mind is actually completely included in another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we've tried to understand, without obviously having the documents, how they fit together; but they are called A and B in your paragraph 1 of the notice. And A is a report prepared for the case of Krajisnik updated for the case of Mico Stanisic, and that update is 29th February, 2008. Then item B is referred to as an addendum prepared for the case of Stanisic and Simatovic but dated the 30th of July, 2004, so somewhere in the middle of the compilation of the other one. Now, at first blush that doesn't look like the most consistent and helpful way of presenting this material. Can you elaborate on how this is being done and why in particular we do not see here a report prepared for the case against Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all both the Krajisnik case and the Mico Stanisic case relate to 1992 and that's why this reports -- these reports concentrate on this. While Stanisic, Simatovic relates to later date as well. So that's why we have two different reports here. That's for the later years; B is for the later years. And why we did not ask for a new report, it's just a matter of time. The expert is no longer working in the Office of the Prosecutor. He has very limited time, and, therefore, we couldn't ask him to prepare an entirely new report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you convinced that there isn't even cutting and pasting you can do with this to put it together in an even more coherent form for everyone that is clearly aimed at relating directly to the case against this accused which is plainly a combination of cases against other accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If we do a cut and paste, we would actually have the -- Mr. Nielsen have to adopt this. But what I think is, rather, a more practical approach is if we for instance say we want to relate only on section A, C, and D of the report, is that perhaps a way forward? If we say we don't want to rely on all of this report but on sections only?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I'm getting even more concerned that you haven't -- in all the time that's been available, been able to get the expert who is going to have to come here and give his evidence, or at least have it presented in a form that he is satisfied with. You haven't got him to take the parts of the report that are relevant directly to the case that you are dealing with here, put them into one report for this case and present it to us in a comprehensive, coherent form. I've encountered this before, and I'm trying to avoid encountering the problems that go with this again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one issue though. The Mico Stanisic is actually one when you get the pre-trial brief, he is one where we basically claim whatever this man did and whatever relates to him relates equally to Mr. Karadzic because he was a subordinate to Mr. Karadzic. At least de facto. And therefore the entire Mico Stanisic report is actually also applies to Mr. Karadzic. And it's the same with Mr. Krajisnik. Only in relation to Stanisic, Simatovic, that's a different issue. But in relation to the number A, it entirely relates to Mr. Karadzic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what I think you might consider doing in relation to this is to let us have the documents that are referred to in this notice immediately following this meeting, and provide us with a short note, if it's appropriate, of the areas of these reports to which you intend to confine your case, because it sound as though that's what you are doing. So this in fact is a statement that you are giving us material, you are not actually going to rely on at the time of the trial. You are going to confine yourself to certain elements of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct in relation to the report B. Because the report B has actually a lot of details. I mean, we want to rely at this moment on both reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But should we not be entitled to a document properly prepared for this case which are confined to the elements of the investigations that the experts have done that relate directly to this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What we feared was when we want an addendum from Mr. Nielsen, this would cause a much greater delay than providing those two reports that he has already done and basically, as for instance, for the report B, relate a lot to actions of Stanisic, Simatovic not related to Mr. Karadzic, that's in particular the Croatia section in that report B. If we would have asked Mr. Nielsen to reconstruct this addendum just fitting for the Karadzic case, this would take him another two months, and that's why we thought it's much faster and most expeditious to provide these two reports that already existing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask you then, how is it you expect judges presented with the material which they are at the moment not familiar with at all, to do that same exercise in less than two months? In fact, we'll be hoping to do it much more expeditiously than that. Why should we be faced with the task of doing it and not the expert himself?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You are correct, but the problem is when the expert tells us, I need another two months to do that, that was our fear, that you would then say no, that's not possible; but we cannot force the expert to give it to us in a week or two. That's our conflict we find ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's one way of viewing it, which may well be correct, but a cynical person might think that perhaps lack of preparation and organisation may have contributed to that situation. Would it be unreasonable to think that there may have been some element of that involved?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't know what to say to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any comment to make on this particular subject?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, and with all your leave and with all due respect, I would leave my comments for a public hearing. So far I have been satisfied with how the things are progressing and therefore I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that point of view. And you are entitled to that. You will not have unlimited scope just to make a show in public in light of what may have emerged here. Anything that happens in public will be with a purpose and an aim that is forensic and not any other. And therefore, one of the things you may seek to do here, without in any way inhibiting the opportunities you will have in public, will be to seek any additional information you want on the subject, and please bear that in mind each time we deal with one of these. Just give the Judges a moment to -- for a brief -- in fact I think what we may do in light of -- no, I think the best plan might be to go through the three that have already been notified, then I think we'll have a short adjournment and discussion among ourselves before we continue with the meeting. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wanted to say was that regardless of my need for everything to be done in public because I see the public as my ally in this particular case, that the issue of expert witness is a hugely important witness -- question. There are 26 of them and some of them are really would be a treat. I won't like to disqualify any of them before the trial because they will provide an excellent opportunity to the Defence to show what is being done. So such a hugely important issue such as expert witness, I don't want to be stifled in private meetings. I hope you understand my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the second one that's been notified, and that's Andras Reidlmayer. Now, there the notice, the summary indicated that there would be five reports or addenda, and one statement; and we have I think five in total; is that correct? Including a database.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Four. So three expert reports and a statistical addendum. Now, does that mean there is no statement to follow?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't really understand. What do you mean statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in your summary, this summary list, against Reidlmayer you say that you would be producing five reports or addenda and one statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That relates only to disclosure. That's not what we filed. It's showing what is disclosed and what is still to be translated. It has nothing to do with actual reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, there is plainly -- perhaps plainly stating it too high, it would appear that there may be some overlap between B1 and C, it's not complete overlap but some of the municipalities are the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, there is overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a difference between the reports or is it genuinely repetition?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The reports rely in relation to monuments and buildings that are discussed, that's why -- and looking at our schedule D when we want to cover all the sites in schedule D, we had to provide all these reports, otherwise, it would not be complete. And with Mr. Reidlmayer, it's the same issue of preparing an additional, a focused Karadzic report would actually take more time than looking at those reports just at the sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in the report prepared for the case of Krajisnik when compared with the report prepared for the case of Seselj, will we find identical language relating to the same buildings?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think so, yes but I cannot be a hundred per cent sure because I didn't compare them, so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in relation to number a, which is -- well, which relates to Bosnia-Herzegovina and selected municipalities, and C, which again relates to Bosnia-Herzegovina but non-Serb cultural heritage and certain municipalities, is it possible there's also overlap there?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And just one final question I have on this one, the fourth item, number D, the underlying database, compiled by Andras Reidlmayer and which his reports are based, what is the general nature of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Reidlmayer has actually compiled a programme covering all his findings, so what he usually would do, he would have this programme available in court and if there is a question to a particular site, he can immediately call it up and we would see it on the screens, and he could answer particular questions directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I didn't catch the first part of that, can you tell me again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He has his -- he has a particular database covering all these sites, and he can call it up in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the third one now, the notice relating to Dr. Kathryn Barr, who is a handwriting expert. Now, can you help us by indicating how this evidence fits into the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can address that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Barr is, as you say, a handwriting expert and in the previous Srebrenica trials she has analysed handwriting which appears in an important exhibit in our submission which is the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook. Without going into the substance, it's a notebook written by various -- written and drafted by various members of the Zvornik Brigade at different times that they were on duty. And it is essentially an exercise in authenticating this exhibit, which has been challenged in the past, as well as indicating which officers of the Zvornik Brigade were on duty in performing various actions at different times during the height of the murders in the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do the different dates demonstrate the history of the obtaining of samples, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The different dates I think is that as issues arose, a different part of the book would be analysed. I'm just waiting for the translation. In addition, Ms. Barr has analysed vehicle logs, gasoline logs, and items of that nature seized from the Zvornik Brigade, and I believe the Drina Corps, to authenticate the handwriting of different officers and different individuals on those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any overlap among these reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I believe not. You can see they are quite short. The first one I can see by the English ERN range is approximately seven pages. That's the report of Dragan Jokic of 2003 dated 16 July. Next one in the notice B, is about six pages. So this is, I would think, fairly non-controversial evidence. It's different parts of one big exhibit and other exhibits to authenticate that the people who we say wrote on these exhibits or signed these documents in fact did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, I think we will adjourn briefly just now. Before we do, is there anything you want to ask or say about the matters that we've been discussing so far?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you'll excuse us, we'll be probably no more than 20 minutes. Say we'll resume at 3.30. Someone will make sure that you're comfortable meanwhile, once we withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are missing one -- she's not returning. Maybe this is an appropriate time then to record that the first liaison officer, Jelena Gurduvic, was present during the first part of the meeting and has now left and that the Registry court deputy present is Yaiza Alvarez and has been since the beginning of the meeting. I want to return just briefly to a question on which I think we are not clear on the moment and that is the exact nature of the database of Mr. Reidlmayer, can you tell me again, please, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, how that differs from the reports themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The database that Mr. Reidlmayer has does also include a lot of photographic evidence. That's the key -- that's the main difference as far as I remember. I haven't looked, I must admit, I haven't looked at the database. It's a long time ago that I saw it, therefore, I think that the key difference is the amount of photographic evidence that he has on the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we would like you to do then, in relation to these three experts is to now give copies of all the documents referred to in these three filings to the Trial Chamber with a note of the parts of the documents on which you do not intend to found in the trial. Are you able to do that fairly expeditiously?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously we want to have a chance to look at these documents before the Status Conference, and it may be that we would want to react in some way, but we would only do that obviously in the course of the status conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The only problem that I see when we have to produce that before the Status Conference, we are already under enormous pressure because of the interims pre-trial brief, so to get this in addition, would cause a problem; but I will actually have to regress later on in relation to this interim pre-trial brief and if we -- one of them would be an extension of time of one week for the interims pre-trial brief if that would be acceptable, then I think we could manage. But if we have to produce the pre-trial brief on the 30th, I don't think we can manage that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's not simply a question of giving us electronic copies of the various documents and identifying in them the parts that you don't intend to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The problem is only that we now would have to -- we can produce the electronic version, even a printed version; but to review it again and see which -- exactly which parts we would not want to rely, on is a bit of a tricky issue. Because just as an example, the number B for Nielsen, we cannot say just generally we are not relying on anything that relates to Croatia because we are actually claiming here a JCE with an over-arching JCE with Milosevic in there, with Jovica Stanisic in there. So there is JCE related evidence that actually is based on Croatia events that we would now have to now distinguish between what is necessary, what is not necessary. So we have to go carefully through that report B for Stanisic, Simatovic, and distract these JCE related passages. So that's why it's just going through the reports again. For Reidlmayer it would be easier, but for Stanisic, Simatovic for Nielsen reports it would be -- it would take quite some time. And unfortunately for people that deal with these expert reports and filings are also the ones that are drafting the interims brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two out of three is not bad, so you can produce to us, please, the material in relation to Barr and Reidlmayer with a note on the parts on which you don't intend to rely. Please give us the material in relation to Nielsen. We would prefer all of them in electronic form so that we can do the printing ourselves as necessary; and we can only ask you to use your best endeavours in relation to Nielsen. But I think you can take it that the subject of how you are compiling and putting together the material in relation to these experts is not a dead issue and is likely to feature in the discussion also at the Status Conference. To what extent will become clear as we proceed through this list you gave us of the experts. The very first one on your list was a Jose Baraybar, in respect of whom there are said to be in existence 14 reports and addenda and two statements. Now, are you able to indicate to us how you are likely to produce the material in relation to him? Is that again, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, I think I can say that again this -- these reports and examinations various times are all related to different parts of the Srebrenica portion of the case. We will need to find out whether they are accepted. In many ways, again, it may not be a contested issue, as these are scientific reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are these individual reports relating to different grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean overlap is unlikely?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As regards to, I believe I can say with confidence, with regards to all of the Srebrenica scientific reports, the pathological reports, and anthropological reports, there is not overlap. Because of the nature of the way the investigation was conducted over time, different mass graves examined at different times by different experts, different graves discovered at different times, and the nature of primary and secondary graves, throughout the time different reports by different experts have been created but they do not overlap. In other words, we don't have two expert reports which concern a grave at Cerska or Lazete 2 with overlapping evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we still on track then for Baraybar, John Clark, Christopher Lawrence, and Freddy Peccerelli all to the filed by the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've now found my correct notes. Baraybar, yes, 1st of April. Lawrence should be 1st of April. Haglund, I believe also 1st of April, with one translation issue. And I hope I haven't missed one. Clark as well, 1st of April. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say one translation issue, the indication was there was a substantial amount to be translated for Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, and if I can take a moment to explain that. Dr. Haglund attached to his report the individual autopsy reports which form the basis of the report. In the previous Srebrenica cases, those have not been translated. For all the experts, there were individual reports per body, per skeleton examining what was found in that numbered grave, so there was a huge amount of individual reports for these experts. Most of the experts, with the exception of Haglund, did not attach those and make them part of their report. So with all those experts, the underlying individual reports for each body or set of remains in a mass grave are disclosed, of course, but they don't form a part of the body of the report. I would hope that we don't need to translate into B/C/S these, over 1500 pages of individual reports which Haglund attached. We haven't done so for the others, which were not attached and they haven't been previously. These individual reports follow a format explaining the clothing found on this particular victim, the personal effects, whether he had a watch or tobacco, things like that. So they are rather simple and follow that format, and that's perhaps something that Dr. Karadzic can comment on, whether he -- if he wishes, whether he insists on each and every one of these being translated. They haven't been in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He has made it clear, that's the sort of thing he won't comment on today, so there's no point in my raising that with him. But in relation to Haglund, you referred to 11 reports and addenda and eight documents, I presume they are additional documents which comprise the 940 pages yet to be translated. Now, are you saying that they are in a position to be disclosed in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, these are the annexes to the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you should make that disclosure if you haven't already done so, I would suggest, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have done the disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So disclosure as you would have it at least for these various persons that you've mentioned, will be achieved before the Status Conference. The other one you didn't mention was Freddy Peccerelli who seems to be also an anthropology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, there's a similar issue, although the outstanding number of pages is less than that for Dr. Haglund. Mr. Peccerelli also attached to his report extensive materials which are not -- which often are not attached as part of the body of the report, so it's the same situation but a smaller number of pages; and our position would be the same that it hasn't been translated in the past and we hope not to be required do so in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should meanwhile follow the same course if you haven't already done so. I can't remember now if you mentioned Richard Wright or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe I did, Your Honour, that should be ready for the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps we should just finish with -- no, in fact, I think that does complete the pathology-related material. Another category -- sorry, I think you should give the Trial Chamber also electronic copies of all of these materials now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next category of expert is referred to as military analyst. Number 3 is the first example, and then there are other examples at 17, 19, and 24. Now, there may be no objection to you corroborating some of your evidence, but can you help me on the need for four military analysts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these analysts do not basically overlap. They cannot be excluded that in all of them there may be a reference to Supreme Command or something like that. However, they all have very distinct topics. Mr. Brown for instance will speak about the military events in the ARK. And while Mr. Phillipps will speak and his report will relate to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Mr. Butler who is one of the -- it is actually the 26 Rule 70 witness who has now been cleared so I can use his name; Mr. Butler will deal with Srebrenica; and Mr. Theunens will deal with the JNA VRS paramilitary structures all over but except for those particular regions I just mentioned. So there is no overlap between those. There's also a General Vegh that's number 24, he is actually the command and control expert who actually was a top military commander. So there is no overlap of these. We have actually considered, and that's why we actually have added Mr. Phillipps at a later date, we have actually considered whether Mr. Theunens would be our overall expert and could address all these topics but that would mean that he would get familiar with all these particular military scenarios and that would take a lot more time than having the experts that have already dealt and have all the knowledge on these particular war theatres, it's better to have them also instead Mr. Theunens adopting everything and having to get up to speed in all possible matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we going to see the same scenario that there will be a report prepared for one case and then a supplementary report for another case before the Tribunal and the use of parts of each of them, is that going to be a feature of this part of the case as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's -- the -- as you can see, some of these experts are currently producing addendums specifically relating to the role of Dr. Karadzic in this, but they would -- these would actually be addendums to previous reports, so we would tender the previous report plus the addendum. But what we could of course do is we could specify whether we would not want to rely on certain topics. For instance, just as an example, Mr. Theunens has, of course, done an extensive military report in the Milosevic case which deals a lot with Croatia events and only parts of these events as it comes to the mission of the JNA on how it changed over time, that is of course important for the JCE aspects, but other aspects and details would not be needed. So we could actually identify those sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is going to be helpful, I think, to the Trial Chamber at the Status Conference if you can really explain to us what is so difficult for your experts in using their electronic versions and taking out the bits that don't relate to this case and compiling a version of the report, using the material they already have, that relates directly to this case. We -- in our discussions and also in our debate with you this afternoon we are all finding it difficult to understand why that cannot be done. You know from your own experience how difficult it is to keep control of the massive number of documents that will be a feature of this case, and it seems almost a scheme designed to complicate the case to have large numbers of reports rather than to try and consolidate the knowledge and information available to the experts into one. So we will undoubtedly again return to that subject at a later stage. Now, moving through your -- yes, I think in relation to the military analysts, as you make a submission in terms of Rule 94 bis, you should also give us copies of the documents that are referred to in the notice. Now, the next category you refer to is Dr. Johan De Koeijer, forensic document expert. Now, does he do something different from handwriting analysis? Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. He does, Your Honour, this is I believe again a fairly simple and not very controversial report that he has prepared. It is principally analysing marks on paper. So it's not handwriting, but there is a particular, again, military document from the Zvornik Brigade that he has gone through and is able to forensically show that that document has been altered. That entries on the document were erased, and that above them different entries were written in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, from the number of reports, et cetera, referred to there, he has done this on more than one occasion. When you come to notify the accused of the report that's being relied upon in this case, will that refer to one report, or will it be again a series of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we are going to be relying on two reports. The one that I'm afraid I don't remember the content of both of them completely. One is a roster showing who was on duty, and where they went that day, again related to Srebrenica, the other I will have to check. But it will be two reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again we'll have that by the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That should be no problem, Your Honour. And we will disclose this to the Chamber as well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the only other one I think I've not addressed so far on this page is Berko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is actually a ballistic expert, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other one is Richard Higgs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And the difference between the two is Mr. Zecevic will only deal with the shelling Markale 1, while Mr. Higgs will deal with all other shellings. In addition to the shelling Markale 1, Mr. Zecevic will also deal with air-bombs. These are the two subjects that he will deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose a related subject might be sniping, number 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the expert who deals with all sniping incidents that we have in that schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's Sarajevo and therefore completely discrete from the other two?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He is actually the only sniping expert. The other two is also Sarajevo, but it's shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The picture again should be clear by the 1st of April because we should have at least Mr. Zecevic's material. Going over the page, we have two demographers, numbers 13 and 18. And I expressed concern before about the extent of the material here, so what is the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau has actually -- is in the process of preparing new reports for the overall Bosnia, for Sarajevo, and for Srebrenica. We will rely on these new reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Done for this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And in relation to the others, it's just disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it does say that these reports relate to three separate subjects, Sarajevo, Srebrenica, and displacement, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Displaced persons, yes. Internally displaced persons. That's the change in the demographics all over Bosnia, in the 27 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what about Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Brunborg is preparing a report on Srebrenica missing persons and identifications. We are expecting his report for this case. It's -- he did -- it's essentially an update based on new identifications which have been made of missing persons. We are expecting that on the 9th of April, and it will then need to be translated. He is working on that report now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 9th of April may not be unrealistic, but I notice the first date the 1st of May for Ms. Tabeau in a situation which can only be rejigging of information that she's long had. That does not sound a realistic date.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have actually discussed the possibilities of producing reports as soon as possible, and that's what she can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have in your mind a date for this trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we actually thought the trial would start before the summer break. That is what thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you still think on that basis, the 1st of May, for the production of this sort of material is realistic when much more urgent material and material that's likely to form an earlier part of the case is likely to require concentration at that time. You'll have to produce a great many statements which we'll come to in a moment, the accused has to have time to digest the contents of these and work on them, and here we have material which should be capable of fairly ready presentation that could be dealt with in a more leisurely fashion when he has the time to do it rather than all in a rush at the last minute. So I think we are all agreed in saying to you that it would help to alert expert witnesses to the concern of the Chamber that the reworking of already available material should be done more quickly than some of the time-scales you've given us. Some I expect are absolutely okay. But others we are concerned about. Now, we move to a different area, but there are a number of -- well, they are not directly related, but we are into territory which is rather different from the territory we've been looking at so far, and we start with a historian at number 14. There's another one at number 22. Can you assist us with an indication of why we should need historians at this stage in the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, these historians, they deal with very concrete subjects. This is why we have not -- that's why we have two. Mr. Donia deals with two topics, that's the origin of the RS. It's putting historical context to developments in Bosnia. And it's actually starting a long time before the war. So he has really -- is looking at the origins of the RS and the underlying streams. And the other topic he has is the historical context related to Sarajevo and the importance of Sarajevo. While, Mr. Treanor will deal with organs, organs of the RS on the republic level, and their actions and development -- the historical context but very actually very close to the outbreak of the war, and during the war. That's the difference between the two. There's definitely perhaps a bit of overlap, but not particularly much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Then we have what is described as Crisis Staff analysis by Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, she will actually deal with the organs involved in the crimes on the local level and the context and their development. That's her topic. While, Ms. -- yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these three experts, are we, again, going to find that they have given evidence in earlier cases and that we are going to be expected to make use of the material that was produced for the other cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, Ms. Hanson is preparing an entirely new report. Mr. Donia is producing a supplemental report which is actually a -- he is pulling all the material that relates to this case from his previous reports into a new report and adds things. That's actually what you yourself would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He is actually doing this at the moment. And Mr. Treanor is also preparing three new reports, I think. Two, sorry, two new reports. At the moment maybe Ms. Sutherland can help me, I don't know how much we want to rely also on previous reports or whether he pulls it all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Treanor is doing an addendum to the Krajisnik report and also a new report dealing with the Serb leadership and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We are almost there, I think. Propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson is preparing a new report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the nature of his expertise?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think he is a sociologist. He is a sociologist. He has already provided a propaganda report in the Krajisnik case, and he actually looks at the messages and themes coming from the Bosnian Serb leadership and what -- how -- how this message would be received by an audience, by the targeted audience. That's his issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that an area of expertise that's already been accepted at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that we had a propaganda expert in the Milosevic case, Slobodan Milosevic case, and we also had a propaganda expert in the Seselj case. And of course in the Krajisnik case, Mr. Thompson himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt your thoughts. Before we move on, I see that because Mr. Butler was not cleared before, you don't have the information for him on number 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll come to these two before we -- 25 and 26 before we finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Torkildsen is said to deal with financial analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen will address matters that relate to the support provided by the SFRY and the FRY to the Bosnian Serb leadership and the army. He has a very concise, small issue to deal with and it relates basically and we need this evidence for the JCE aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And that leaves the final two, one who has now been identified, that's number 26. Now, Mr. Nicholls, what do you say -- want to say about Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before we moved on, he is preparing an addendum to his previous Srebrenica reports. He has done a report on the events in Srebrenica in July 1995 and at some period before and after July 1995 regarding the events that are pertinent to that part of the indictment. He has also done reports on the structure of the VRS, the Army Republika Srpska, different levels, the Main Staff, corps and Brigade which we intend to introduce. However, he has not worked for the Tribunal for some time. He works and lives in United States. And we have asked him to prepare and addendum based on new material which has been received, new documents since he was here. And all of his previous reports, I believe, are relevant, and we would rely on them, but I -- the addendum will not be ready by 1 April, and we, I have to say, do not expect that addendum until sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've indicated 31st of May, and that would undoubtedly concern us. Now, have you an identity yet for the 25th on the list?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. The problem is still that the outstanding Rule 70 clearance, but we expect it to reach us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a surprising subject to be the subject of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's true, but it's Rule 70 protected witness nevertheless, and but we have actually already agreed with the provider, and we think we received the okay tomorrow. There's one correction I have to make in relation to number 20, Mr. Thompson. The date is wrong, it has to be 31st of April, not May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, there is one other that did concern us and that is number 23, Mr. van der Wijden, and the 15th of May, that seemed a long way away for what he was reporting on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We will check that. I don't know why it is scheduled for the 15th of May. I can't say right now. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just add in relation to Mr. Treanor, I said that he was doing an addendum to the Krajisnik report that deals with 1992, the addendum is in fact covering the period 1993, 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Karadzic, is there anything you want to say on the subject of expert witnesses or to raise with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to leave that for a public hearing, and I fully trust your assessment as to the opportunity and the possibility for the Defence to deal with such a huge volume of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to deal with another aspect that was referred to in your response to our inquiry, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, about disclosure, and you identified another category of witness that was international witnesses, of which you said there would be 60. In replying, though, between dealing with experts and moving on to the international witnesses, you made reference to the disclosure of materials for two witnesses other than experts. Do they fall into this group of 60 international witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. They are actually specific. These are two -- how shall I put it, they are not really experts both, but they have dealt with medical experts. Actually, the ones that we have listed and just discussed. And they dealt with the exhumation reports, and on the Bosnia level, it's Mr. Masovic he can actually give evidence on exhumations not related to medical, the medical expertise in it. And the other one is -- is related to Srebrenica, it's Mr. Manning who was actually our investigator who dealt with investigations. In other cases, in fact, those two have testified and have relied and produced expert reports of these experts that we just, the medical experts that we just have discussed, and these medical expert then actually had not been called. So we would actually wish to hear from Mr. Karadzic at some point in time whether he really -- whether we really need to call all these forensic experts, or whether we can deal with their evidence in the context of having Mr. Masovic and Mr. Manning address the mass graves and then introduce these kind of findings through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we move then to the international witnesses. You initially indicated that for 17 you were subject to Rule 70 restriction. Has that changed?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have actually produced also a document for everyone present here similar to the one for the experts, and we can distribute it. It shows the current situation with the international witnesses. Two for you. So you can actually see in this schedule where we stand with these witnesses, and we have also indicated what the topic of their testimony is. And currently we have only three, is it three, three witnesses for which we don't have Rule 70 clearance yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed what you said there about clearance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, clearance. According to the current situation, we have only three international witnesses for which we are awaiting clearance. For everyone else we have received the clearance. As you can see, we have 50 -- for 50 experts we have disclosed all materials in English, and for ten witnesses, we still have a few items not disclosed because we are awaiting clearance. You can see two -- when you look at the document, the pages 1 to 7 first item relate to those where we have disclosed the English completely, and the rest, the next page, deals with where we have some outstanding disclosure to do in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What percentage of these witnesses have given evidence before on the same topic more or less?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Quite a significant number have given testimony. Those dealing with hostages, you can see in the topic line where we have hostages, these are witnesses that have not testified yet. They actually relate only to these hostages, and that was never a topic here in the Tribunal. But most of the others have given testimony in actually some cases in particular, the Sarajevo Galic case and Dragomir Milosevic case. THE COURT: Where a pseudonym is referred to, has the issue of protective measures already been dealt with in another case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These are witnesses that have protective measures or for which protective measures will be sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some of them relate to hostages?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. It's actually the -- these were previous Rule 70 witnesses and the provider has actually requested that these witnesses will have -- should have pseudonym, so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you intend to rely upon them, then there's no real reason why you should not make fairly early application for protective measures. Thank you for providing that very helpful list. It may give rise to questions in due course, but on the face of it it does provide considerable assistance to the Trial Chamber. The note I was referring to earlier, the e-mail exchange also referred to other witnesses; and you indicated that you had disclosed most material in relation to other witnesses and where you hadn't, then the statements were mostly available. Has the situation changed at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the other witnesses, the situation has not changed because we were disclosing the internationals. However, within the -- until the next disclosure report, we think we will have disclosed 80 of these other witnesses, and our intention is actually to disclose all weeks after the filing of the witness list as the latest. The problem is our limited resources. Therefore, we just have to do it step after step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You probably know by now you are not going to get a great deal of sympathy, certainly speaking for myself, about applying limited resources to this case. So I think one message you may wish to take back from today's meeting is the intensity with which this case is being prepared and the expectation that the resources necessary to meet the Trial Chamber's expectations will be provided. Now, the -- what do you anticipate being the overall total of the other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the moment on our witness list we have 490 witnesses, but that includes the experts and the internationals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but you've -- they account for about 90, and you've told us you've disclosed 80 others, so that's 170, so not far short of 300 short. Are you seriously expecting to lead 460 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, actually a huge amount of these witnesses we actually intend to produce in written format, 92 bis, and we are currently preparing these motions. And there's also one other issue, at the moment we don't know how many adjudicated facts we will -- will be accepted by the Trial Chamber. So in the moment when we have an adjudicated fact accepted, we can drop the witness standing against this adjudicated fact. These are all on the witness list under the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know of any case in which an adjudicated fact has been admitted into evidence before the trial started?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, you'll appreciate the problems of the rule into which we will not go into detail just now and we will have a proper discussion of this in open forum or alternatively in written submissions in relation to your motions; but you must appreciate the Trial Chambers have struggled with adjudicated facts because it's very difficult to know what other evidence might be given in the case that has a bearing on the fact, the adjudicated fact even when admitted is only a presumption which is rebuttable. A Trial Chamber could spend an inordinate amount of time analysing the facts that you've already tendered because there are a number of legal requirements before they are even open for consideration as adjudicated facts, and one has to question the value of the exercise. I appreciate the sentiment behind it, and I would be first in the queue of those asking Trial Chambers to please not revisit issues that have been adjudicated before in cases and in proposing acceptance, it would be a complete and utter waste of time to do otherwise; but it's very difficult within the jurisprudence of this Tribunal to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts, if at all possible, before the trial starts, very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that in the Perisic case, the Trial Chamber took judicial notice of facts relating to Zagreb and Sarajevo before the trial began, and also in the Mico Stanisic case a large number facts over 800 have been accepted at this stage by the Chamber pre trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Facts of what nature? Not that the grass is green now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Background facts, facts relating to the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Actual crime-based evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is presumably on the basis that the Prosecution will lead no more evidence about it, but the Defence may yet challenge it; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't know in relation to Mico Stanisic what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 800 facts have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that apply to the conjoined trial of Stanisic and Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think the decision was December 14th, 2006, so it may have been before Zupljanin was brought into custody. But over a number of different municipalities and dealing with background and armed forces and such and so forth, and the political parties. And in the Perisic case, there was the adjudicated facts for Srebrenica -- sorry, I misspoke, in relation to Sarajevo and Zagreb - and there was none filed in relation to Srebrenica because there was agreed facts in relation to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's interesting. Thank you. Now, of the 300 or just under 300 witnesses whose statements may not have been disclosed, are the statements actually available?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would say most of them are available, yes. But there are still a few witnesses where we don't have statements, and actually, one of them is here even listed in this list, I think here we have also one ... Yes, for instance number 56 when you see here, we are in contact with this gentleman, but we don't have a statement yet. And there are a few other -- others where we don't have a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I'm referring to the others who are not on any of these lists. The almost 300 that you referred to earlier, what is the position with statements for them?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We should have these statements, yes. For some of these witnesses, we do not have yet filed the protective measures motion because for some of them we actually do still speak with the witnesses about; and as soon as we've done that, we can disclose them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But my question really relates not so much to disclosure but availability of these statements. If we ordered you to disclose statements of all these witnesses in seven days, would you be able to do it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You would simply disclose what you have, but the question is roughly, I mean, are there a lot of them where statements are going to filter through later in the process between a 65 ter notice submission and the actual start of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to crime-based witnesses, no, there is another category of witnesses and that is the insider witnesses and there is still follow-up in relation to those witnesses. But with respect to crime based, those are available and can be disclosed. It's simply a matter of getting that job done. We prioritize the experts and internationals first, and now we are turning to the other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. That completes item 5. The Chamber's reviewed the outstanding motions, but has not identified any particular administrative issue that would be appropriate to discuss here. Is there anything you have to raise -- we will come to your question about the pre-trial brief shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Perhaps the only issue, the -- yesterday, I think, yesterday we got this motion Karadzic extension of time for Rule 70 motion regarding alleged Holbrooke agreement. The Prosecution would not oppose this, I don't know whether you want this in writing filed, otherwise it's perhaps it's enough that we declare it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's enough, that you do so, and we will consider the motion in the light of that. Thank you for that. Are there any administrative issues, Mr. Karadzic, in relation to any of the various motions that are now pending that you wish to raise with us here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not much that I would like to point out today. I just wish to reiterate why don't you look at my resources and what resources I have available. I don't have a team, a Defence team set up yet, and I'm wondering how is that going to look once the material starts pouring in. You have a motion concerning equality of arms and resources, and we are waiting to see what you are going to rule regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think following your own lead, this is not the place for a discussion of that nature today in view of the attitude you've taken, which I understand, I'm not at this moment meaning to criticize, and I would rather in view of what you said earlier, have that discussion in open court in the Status Conference insofar as its necessary. But it may be that if we have another meeting of this nature with the experience of today, you may feel more comfortable in engaging more broadly in discussion. I'm simply asking you to reflect on that; I'm not suggesting you have to change your mind just now for one moment. The seventh item on the agenda was to discuss in general terms what plan will be required under Rule 65 ter (D)(ii) if I can explain Mr. Karadzic, the pre-trial judge should establish a plan of work for the preparation of the case leading up to the trial. It would have been pointless trying to do this much before now, because of the delay in dealing with the amendment to the indictment. And there are other obstacles currently in the way of dealing with this too including outstanding business which is subject of attention in the Appeals Chamber, and also the motions that we have to deal with. But we do intend to produce a work-plan and hopefully can do so certainly if not before the Status Conference, immediately after the Status Conference. I need to find my copy before I can -- yeah. Yeah, I think one date I would invite your comment on, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff; we have in mind at the moment ordering full disclosure of statements insofar as that has not been done by the end of April. Would you be uncomfortable with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The only problem that I see is the B/C/S transcripts. We can disclose whatever we have, the statements and everything, the statements and the transcripts, but if it comes to -- if you would order us to disclose the B/C/S transcripts, we would have -- I don't think we could do that because we have actually calculated and looked at what we would have to -- which figures we would have for the experts, for instance. For the experts, we have 8.000 pages transcriptions of which we have done 25 per cent. For the international witness it's 13.000 pages transcripts, and for the other witnesses we can only say that it's also a considerable amount. And although we have a group of 15 transcribers working, it's something of six to ten months if we would have to do that, and that we could not manage to do until the end of April. Everything else, yes. And I recall that there is a -- there was a mechanism in place in the Seselj case that dealt with transcriptions, and they were actually only to be produced some very short period before the witness actually testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's plainly a matter that will have to be dealt with at the Status Conference. So I think we will probably postpone the production of the work-plan until after the Status Conference, but you can take it that we will also be aiming at a final pre-trial brief and lists, a significant period before any Pre-trial Conference; so we are not talking about the basic six weeks in this case. We'll be working for lists earlier. But you are well on the way, obviously, to providing lists and having had the useful discipline of preparing an interim pre-trial brief, you will be well on the way to produce that also. But we will have some discussion of that at the Status Conference before these dates are fixed. Now, Mr. Karadzic, is there anything you want to say on the subject of a work-plan, and in particular just the two subjects we've mentioned under that heading, that's the dead-line for witness statements, and when a full list of witnesses and exhibits from the Prosecution should be submitted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me this opportunity. For the time being, I would just like to say that your decision to draw up the plan after the Status Conference, at the Status Conference which I've had an opportunity to review all the possibilities available to both the Defence and the OTP and see where we are exactly in this whole jungle of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the final item on this agenda is the matter that the Prosecution asked to be added, which was discussion of the filing of the interim pre-trial brief. Now, you'll remember that at a previous hearing, I ordered this, it's not something that is always done, but it was done with the objective of setting out as clearly as possible at an earlier stage what the Prosecution theory of the case against you is, and what the material is that they will be relying on. And indication has been given that they are finding the dead-line of the 30th of March tight, was it 31st of March, tight. In keeping with your earlier position, this is perhaps something you think ought not to be discussed at this meeting. Is that your position, or are you happy if we hear from the Prosecution the basis on which they seek that additional time? The alternative is to ask them to make an application in writing and we would deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this not going to be the subject at the Status Conference, I have no objection to hearing that, but I cannot express my view today. It is customary that once the OTP applies for certain delay for a certain -- for a number of days, the Defence had no objection to that, and I also see that OTP does not generally object to any flexibility extended to the issue of dead-lines. However, this is a more serious issue than some motion, and if this is going to be discussed at the Status Conference, then I can give you my final view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is the Status Conference is after the dead-line, that's why it's being raised today. The dead-line, is it the 30th or 31st.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 30th of March, and the Status Conference is the 2nd of April. But if you do not want it dealt with just now, then we will instruct a written submission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will I have a right to reply to that written submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but you would -- if the submission is made tomorrow, you would have until Thursday only to respond, so you would have 24 hours to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then in that case, I would kindly ask for the extension of time for my reply. Anyway, it would be better if I had that in writing, and I would do that best to provide a timely answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we require, you if you want to insist on this application, to make it by written motion; I'm sure you could even secure a late filing today. But the 30th is Monday, so a decision would have to be made on Friday, so the earliest realistic response is end of close of business on Thursday, I am afraid. That would have to be the position, Mr. Karadzic, but we'll deal with that transparently as you require in terms of a written submission and a response.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland just mentioned whether it would be a possibility to make an oral application now and have Mr. Karadzic deal with it in writing? But we also can make a filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It should be done in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is yet another issue. It's not just the request for one week extension, and we will do that today. The other thing is we actually also would want -- want to file a request extension of the word limit, because for three reasons. We have seen the Krajisnik appeal judgement, and seen in how many details actually the Trial Chamber -- or rather the Appeal Chamber wants these matters, in particular JCE matters be dealt with. We have immediately responded to this, and we have substantially added to these details and are adding these details to our interims pretrial brief. However, that really means that we cannot -- we cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. That also has to be done in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any other matter you wish to raise, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As we indicated in the previous order, it's not normal for the transcript of the Rule 65 ter meeting to be made public, but we are content, if you wish, to order that this one be public. It's a matter for you. If you wish it to remain in the normal form as a confidential filing, then so it shall remain. If you wish it to be public, then we will order it to be public. What is your preferred course of action?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every stage of this business I care about the public very much, and in this particular instance, I would like this to be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, is there any part of it that would require to be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't know whether we mentioned any witness now who has actually -- would have protective measures. Could we see it first and then give our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a perfectly reasonable request, that the Prosecution see the transcript and direct our attention to any part that perhaps, for sound reasons, ought not to be public; and what I think we'll do is order that you have the -- you are clear about the position by, well, when will the transcript be available, that's the first thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALVAREZ
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So by Friday of this week so that it's available for the Status Conference. You look as though you wish to say something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that only Mr. Butler's name has been mentioned, if the protective measures are going to be applied to him, otherwise I didn't notice any other names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are probably right, but experience tells us that it does no harm to check; and for the sake of two or three days, I think caution is the appropriate course. I think I speak for the Trial Chamber in expressing our gratitude to the parties for their assistance they have given. I hope that you've detected a flavour of the way in which we would like the pre-trial work to proceed and the cooperation we hope that parties can give each other to try to minimize the pointless examination of material that really is not in issue for the purposes of what is a serious trial on clearly identifiable and identified issues. So I make these remarks obviously subject to any clarification that eventually merges from the indictment, but we all know that this is at least one case before the Tribunal where there are four discrete subject areas and albeit they raise in some instances complex, legal issues, the subject matter is clear; and I hope the parties see that there would be considerable benefit for everybody in ensuring as clear a presentation of this case as possible and to that extent -- for that purpose, cooperation among the parties is really essential. So thank you and we will see all of you again on the 2nd of April when again we shall sit as three judges so that any decisions that need to be made can be made expeditiously.
